title: Week 25 Check-In · By the Great Horn Spoon!
description: This week you learned the real history of the Gold Rush and read Chapters 1 to 3. You practiced prepositional phrases for setting, the roots aud and or, long place names and Gold Rush words, and planning an adventure. Show what you know.

questions.label: Identification
questions.text: Which sentence uses prepositional phrases to tell where something happens?
options: Below decks, in the creaking darkness, two stowaways waited.
questions.status: fixed (four options; the old A and C were not sentences)

questions.label: Add a Phrase
questions.text: Rewrite this sentence. Add a prepositional phrase that tells where or when the action happens.
questions.excerpt: The captain paced and growled to himself.
questions.key: Any prepositional phrase of place or time, e.g. In his cabin, the captain paced and growled to himself.

questions.label: Application
questions.text: Write one sentence about the Lady Wilma's voyage with at least two prepositional phrases. Underline each one.
questions.key: Two or more prepositional phrases, e.g. At dawn, the ship sailed out of Boston harbor.

questions.label: Root
questions.text: Which pair of words both carry the root or, meaning speak?

questions.label: Context Clues
questions.text: Read the sentence from Chapter 2. What does undaunted mean?
questions.excerpt: “The truth of the matter was that neither Jack nor the butler had the slightest idea how to go about catching a thief. But Praiseworthy was undaunted.”
questions.status: replaced (audacious only looks like an aud word; it comes from a Latin word for bold)

questions.label: Use the Word
questions.text: Use the word argonaut in a sentence that shows its link to the Greek myth and to the Gold Rush.
questions.key: A Gold Rush seeker named after Jason's sailors who sailed for the Golden Fleece, e.g. Like the Argonauts of the old myth, the gold-seekers sailed off to find gold.

questions.label: Break It Down
questions.text: Write Patagonia in syllables with dots between them. Then write the loudest syllable in capital letters.

questions.label: Spell It in Context
questions.text: Write one sentence about the Gold Rush that uses one of this week's place names and one Gold Rush word (Argonaut or passenger). Spell both correctly.
questions.key: California, Sacramento, Patagonia or equator + Argonaut or passenger, both spelled correctly.
questions.status: changed (the scope adds Gold Rush words)

questions.label: Comprehension
questions.text: Why do Jack and Praiseworthy end up shoveling coal at the end of Chapter 1?
options: Jack refused to be ship's boy and chose to stay with Praiseworthy.
Captain Swain put them in chains.
They volunteered to fix the boiler.
The cook needed help in the galley.

questions.label: Inference
questions.text: Read the passage from Chapter 2. What does it show about Praiseworthy's plan?
options: The sow could really tell who was dishonest.
The thief was afraid to touch the sow, so his finger stayed clean.
Praiseworthy saw the thief in the dark.
The captain found the money in the thief's cabin.

questions.label: Theme
questions.text: Praiseworthy says, “I was born to my calling” (he means a butler). Yet in Chapters 1–3 he hides in a barrel, shovels coal, and catches a thief. What is one idea the author is showing about who a person really is? Use one detail.
questions.key: A person is more than a job title; character shows in what you do (e.g. he outwits the thief with the coal-dust sow).
questions.from: 25.4 Reading Q3; What Good Readers Do
questions.status: fixed (the quote was invented: “born to be a butler”)

questions.label: Read Like a Writer
questions.text: This sentence states Jack's problem plainly. Write one sentence that states your own hero's problem just as plainly.
questions.excerpt: “And then Jack had overheard Banker Stites tell Aunt Arabella that her inheritance was almost gone.” (Chapter 1)
questions.key: One clear sentence that names the hero and the problem.
questions.status: new (the scope's Read Like a Writer focus)

questions.label: Your Plan
questions.text: Sum up your adventure story plan in 3–5 sentences: your hero, the problem, the setting, and what is at stake.

passage.title: Reading passage (Chapter 2)
passage.text: “But one of you, fearing that the sow's squeal would give you away — one of you approached but didn't touch a finger to her back. Look around you, gentlemen. If there is a man among you without coal dust on his finger — he has exposed himself as the thief!”
passage.cite: Sid Fleischman, By the Great Horn Spoon!, Chapter 2
